definition.text: First-derivative tests that an optimal solution of a nonlinear programming problem must pass, provided certain regularity conditions hold.

facts.text: They extend the method of Lagrange multipliers, which allows only equality constraints, to problems with inequality constraints.
Harold W. Kuhn and Albert W. Tucker published them in 1951; William Karush had stated them in an unpublished 1939 master's thesis.
With no inequality constraints, they reduce to the Lagrange conditions and the KKT multipliers become Lagrange multipliers.
Many optimization algorithms can be read as ways of numerically solving the KKT system of equations and inequalities.
They are also sufficient for an optimum when a maximization's objective is concave, its inequality constraints convex, its equality constraints affine and Slater's condition holds.
Economists use them to get qualitative results, for example that a firm maximizing sales revenue subject to a minimum profit produces where marginal revenue is below marginal cost.
Each multiplier is the rate at which the best achievable value rises as its resource constraint is loosened, an interpretation used in utility maximization.

definition.text: The KKT condition that an inequality constraint which is not binding at the optimum gets a multiplier of zero.

facts.text: It is often written as the product of each multiplier and its constraint being zero.
Picturing the solution as a particle, a constraint can only push back when the particle touches its boundary.

definition.text: A regularity condition that guarantees that the optimum of a constrained problem satisfies the KKT conditions.

facts.text: The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) is the most frequently used.
Slater's condition applies to convex problems: some point must satisfy the inequality constraints strictly.
Weaker qualifications are preferred in practice because they cover more problems.

definition.text: A method for finding the highest or lowest value of a function when the choice variables must satisfy one or more equations exactly.

facts.text: It is named after the mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange.
It turns a constrained problem into one where the ordinary derivative test for unconstrained problems can be used, through a new function called the Lagrangian.
At a constrained optimum, the gradient of the objective is a linear combination of the constraints' gradients.
Each multiplier measures how fast the optimized quantity changes as its constraint is relaxed.
In economic models such as general equilibrium, consumers maximize utility and firms maximize profit under budget and production constraints, usually solved with Lagrange multipliers.
In optimal control, the multipliers become costate variables in Pontryagin's maximum principle.
The principle of maximum entropy used in cost–benefit analysis under uncertainty also relies on Lagrange multipliers.
